Ventricular arrhythmias (refractory)

Uncontrolled clinical evidence reports acute suppression of refractory ventricular arrhythmias in some patients, with incomplete response and recurrence. Two rat studies report reduced arrhythmia incidence or inducibility after myocardial injury.

Evidence summary

What the evidence suggests

Stellate-ganglion phototherapy was followed by acute suppression of electrical storm in some patients in one uncontrolled rescue pilot. Additional case reports describe individual outcomes, while two rat experiments report reduced ventricular-arrhythmia incidence or inducibility after myocardial injury. Comparative clinical efficacy, durability, and survival benefit remain unknown.

Human and clinical evidence

The PBM Database contains one single-arm pilot in 11 patients whose electrical storm had remained refractory to medication, sedation, and catheter ablation. Phototherapy suppressed electrical storm within 72 hours in seven patients. Two other patients had a lower event frequency without full suppression, and two remained in electrical storm. Two of the seven initial responders later had recurrent arrhythmia when maintenance treatment was not continued (Nonoguchi et al. 2021).

A targeted PubMed search identified four directly relevant case-report publications outside the database inventory. They describe use in a patient with a left-ventricular assist device, a patient with cardiac sarcoidosis, a patient requiring mechanical circulatory support, and longer-term outpatient treatment with a portable device. These reports add clinical experience but remain uncontrolled (Sato et al. 2020; Tanabe et al. 2022; Takahashi et al. 2024; Okidono et al. 2025).

Animal evidence

Two rat experiments from one research group used myocardial-infarction and ischemia-reperfusion models. In the post-infarction study, 610 nm LED treatment reduced ventricular premature beats, non-sustained ventricular-tachycardia burden, and the combined incidence of sustained ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation. In the ischemia-reperfusion study, treatment reduced stimulated arrhythmia inducibility. Both experiments also reported lower stellate-ganglion activity and changes in neuroinflammatory or myocardial inflammatory markers (Wang et al. 2019; Wang et al. 2019).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The clinical pilot used either the EXCEL-Xe xenon system with a 400–1,100 nm emission range or the Super Lizer near-infrared system with a 600–1,600 nm range. Treatment was delivered over the stellate-ganglion region for ten minutes, twice weekly for four weeks. Later case reports used different schedules, including daily treatment and portable outpatient exposure. The rat studies used 610 nm LED protocols at 1.7 mW/cm² and 2 J/cm², directed to experimental neural targets. These routes and schedules are not interchangeable, and no comparative dose-finding study has established an optimal regimen.

Interpretation

The clinical evidence suggests that stellate-ganglion phototherapy may acutely reduce arrhythmia burden in selected patients receiving rescue care, but response is not universal and recurrence can occur. The animal studies support biological plausibility. Controlled studies are required to determine added benefit, durability, safety, and effects on survival.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

In the single-arm rescue pilot, electrical storm was suppressed within 72 hours in 7 of 11 patients. Two additional patients had reduced event frequency without full suppression, while 2 of 11 remained in electrical storm. Mean arrhythmia burden changed from 8.0 ± 9.0 to 2.0 ± 5.3 episodes per day (p = 0.066); two initial responders later had recurrence without maintenance treatment (Nonoguchi et al. 2021).

In a cardiac-sarcoidosis case report, anti-tachycardia pacing events decreased from 371 to 25 after stellate-ganglion phototherapy alongside ongoing care (Tanabe et al. 2022).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low certainty for control of refractory ventricular arrhythmia. The clinical evidence is uncontrolled, responses were incomplete or temporary for some patients, and animal studies cannot establish patient benefit.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Certainty is very low because the database evidence contains one uncontrolled 11-patient rescue pilot, and later external reports are single cases. Treatment was added to intensive ongoing care, no sham or usual-care comparator was used, follow-up was limited, and the two animal studies cannot resolve clinical efficacy, recurrence, survival, or safety (Nonoguchi et al. 2021; Wang et al. 2019; Wang et al. 2019).
